resources.string: Original diagrams of a normal capillary. Scale and timing are illustrative; moving highlights trace anatomy, not changes in vessel width.
Endothelial cells line the lumen, the space where blood flows. The pericyte sits on the tissue-facing side of the lining, outside the blood path.
A pericyte sends slender extensions along and partway around the endothelial tube. In this cross-section, the moving highlight follows one extension. The pericyte is not a continuous sleeve.
The two cells share a thin supporting layer called the basement membrane. At some points their surfaces meet directly, as shown at the highlighted contact.
The endothelium forms the inner lining. Pericytes help support the small vessel wall from outside it. Both cell types contribute to the shared basement membrane and help maintain the wall.

A Langerhans cell in the epidermis
Original diagrams of an epidermal immune cell. The diamonds stand for sampled material, not individual molecules. Scale and timing are illustrative.
Langerhans cells are immune sentinels in the epidermis, the outer tissue of the skin. Their cell bodies lie between keratinocytes, beneath the flattened surface layers.
Branching extensions called dendrites can reach and withdraw between keratinocytes. They help the cell sample its surroundings while the cell body remains in the epidermis.
A Langerhans cell can display small pieces of sampled material on its surface. This display, called antigen presentation, lets another immune cell read information about the sample.
A nearby T cell can recognize a displayed piece during cell contact. Interactions like this help regulate local immune activity; contact does not always produce the same response.
